sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1240
text: Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis follows infection by:
explanation: Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows infection by nephritogenic strains of Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (e.g., M-types 12, 49) after a latent interval of 1-4 weeks.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1242
text: Acute diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is due to:
options: Deposition of immune complexes in the glomeruli
explanation: PSGN is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction caused by circulating immune complexes (antigen-antibody) depositing in the subepithelial space as pathognomonic subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1246
text: Nephrotic syndrome is NOT characterised by:
explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is clinically defined by massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/24h), severe hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), generalized edema, and hyperlipidemia with lipiduria. Gross hematuria and hypertension are characteristic of nephritic, not nephrotic, syndrome.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1248
text: Oedema of the nephritic syndrome is due to:
options: Excessive reabsorption of water and salt by the tubules
Increased hydrostatic pressure of the blood
explanation: Edema in nephritic syndrome is primarily caused by primary renal sodium and water retention due to acute reduction in GFR, leading to circulatory overload and periorbital edema.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1252
text: Epithelial crescents are characteristic of:
explanation: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN / crescentic GN) is characterized on light microscopy by circumferential epithelial crescents lining Bowman's space, composed of proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating monocytes/macrophages.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1253
text: Membrano-proliferative glomerulonephritis is characterised by all  EXCEPT:
options: Infiltration of the glomeruli by polymorphs
Thickening of the glomerular capillary walls
explanation: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN Type I) is characterized by mesangial cell interposition and subendothelial immune deposits causing glomerular basement membrane duplication, creating a classic 'tram-track' or split-basement-membrane appearance on Silver stain.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1254
text: The following change(s) occur in minimal change glomerulonephritis:
options: None of the above (glomeruli appear normal on light microscopy)
explanation: Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis) characteristically shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence, but electron microscopy reveals diffuse, uniform effacement (flattening) of podocyte foot processes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1256
text: Subepithelial electron dense deposits are characteristic of:
explanation: Membranous nephropathy is defined ultrastructurally by subepithelial electron-dense immune deposits along the glomerular basement membrane, separated by spikes of silver-staining basement membrane matrix ('spike and dome' pattern).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1267
text: Factors predisposing te pyelonephritis include all EXCEPT:
explanation: Acute pyelonephritis is a suppurative inflammation of the kidney caused predominantly by ascending Gram-negative enteric bacilli (E. coli). Predisposing factors include urinary tract obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, pregnancy, and diabetes mellitus.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1268
text: Females are more susceptible to urinary tract infection because:
options: The immune system is weaker in females
explanation: Females have a marked anatomical predisposition to ascending urinary tract infections and pyelonephritis due to their significantly shorter urethra and its close anatomical proximity to the fecal flora of the anus.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1269
text: Routes of infection in pyelonephritis:
options: Ascending infection from the urinary bladder
Blood spread from a septic focus
explanation: The predominant and most frequent route of renal infection in acute pyelonephritis is ascending infection from the lower urinary tract up the ureters into the renal pelvis and calyces.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1271
text: Individuals who consume large quantities of analgesics may develop:
explanation: Chronic excessive ingestion of analgesic mixtures (phenacetin, aspirin, acetaminophen) causes chronic interstitial nephritis complicated by ischemic renal papillary necrosis, where necrotic papillae slough into the urine causing ureteric colic and hematuria.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1272
text: Mismatched blood transfusion leads to:
explanation: Mismatched ABO blood transfusion triggers massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria, systemic hypotension, and severe ischemic/nephrotoxic Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN), leading to acute oliguric renal failure.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1273
text: Tuberculosis of the kidney is NOT:
explanation: Renal tuberculosis is an active hematogenous metastatic infection secondary to primary pulmonary tuberculosis. It classically begins in the corticomedullary junction, producing caseating fibrocaseous granulomas that cavitate into the calyceal system.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1312
text: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs may lead to:
explanation: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can induce acute interstitial nephritis characterized by tubular cell injury, interstitial edema, and an inflammatory infiltrate rich in eosinophils and T-lymphocytes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1259
text: The gross picture of the kidneys in benign hypertension is similar to that of:
explanation: Benign nephrosclerosis in essential hypertension is characterized grossly by symmetrical, moderately reduced kidneys with a fine, granular, pebbled cortical surface resembling leather ('grain leather' appearance) due to patchy cortical atrophy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1260
text: Flea-bitten kidney is a gross feature of:
explanation: Malignant hypertension is characterized by widespread hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis ('onion-skinning') and necrotizing arteriolitis with fibrinoid necrosis, producing petechial cortical hemorrhages termed a 'flea-bitten' kidney.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1262
text: Diabetic nephropathy does NOT predisposes to:
explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is characterized by diffuse glomerulosclerosis and pathognomonic nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), accompanied by severe arteriolar hyalinosis affecting BOTH afferent and efferent arterioles.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1263
text: The most common type of giomerulonephritis seen in lupus nephritis is:
explanation: In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Class IV Diffuse Proliferative Lupus Nephritis is the most common, most severe, and most aggressive histological subtype, requiring intensive immunosuppressive therapy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1264
text: Wire loop appearance in the glomeruli is characteristic of:
explanation: Wire loop lesions in lupus nephritis represent extensive, confluent subendothelial immune complex deposits that markedly thicken the glomerular capillary walls, resembling rigid bent wires on light microscopy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1265
text: Good-Pasteur’s syndrome is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Most frequent in young adults ~~ E. Pulmonary haemorrhages
explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by circulating autoantibodies directed against the non-collagenous domain (NC1) of alpha-3 chain of collagen type IV in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, producing rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary alveolar hemorrhage.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1274
text: The following thrombus does NOT send emboli to the renal arteries:
explanation: Renal arterial infarction is typically caused by thromboembolism originating from mural thrombi in the left heart (atrial fibrillation, left ventricular MI) or severe atherosclerotic aortic plaques, producing wedge-shaped pale, coagulative cortical infarcts.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1258
text: Gross features of the kidneys in chronic glomerulonephritis include all  EXCEPT:
options: Contraction of the kidneys is asymmetrical
Cut surface shows thick-walled blood vessels
explanation: End-stage chronic glomerulonephritis produces markedly contracted, symmetrically shrunken kidneys with a diffusely granular thinned cortex, obliterated corticomedullary junction, and global hyalinization/sclerosis of glomeruli.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1286
text: The following is a cause of acute renal failure:
explanation: Acute renal failure (acute kidney injury) can result from prerenal hypoperfusion (shock, dehydration), intrinsic acute tubular necrosis (ischemic or toxic), or postrenal acute bilateral urinary tract obstruction.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1238
text: Horse-shoe kidney is a:
explanation: Horseshoe kidney is the most common congenital fusion anomaly, where the lower poles of the kidneys are fused across the midline anterior to the abdominal aorta and IVC, trapped inferiorly by the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1239
text: Adult polycystic kidney is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait
Shows multiple cysts communicating with the pelvis
explanation: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD, PKD1/PKD2 genes) is characterized by bilaterally massively enlarged kidneys filled with multiple non-communicating fluid-filled cysts lined by flattened epithelium, inexorably causing ESRD in adulthood.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1316
text: A male patient with a long history of pulmonary tuberculosis, is now  suffering from chronic renal failure. The most possible cause is:
explanation: In long-standing chronic suppurative or tuberculous disease, renal secondary (AA) amyloidosis develops, manifesting with pale, waxy, enlarged kidneys with positive Congo Red staining showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1317
text: A 40 years old woman presented with chronic renal failure.  Pyelography showed dilation of the pelvicalyceal system. Renal biopsy  revealed tubular atrophy, periglomerular fibrosis and interstitial  inflammatory cells. The most possible diagnosis is:
explanation: Chronic pyelonephritis produces characteristically asymmetric, irregularly scarred kidneys with deep, broad, U-shaped corticomedullary depressions overlying blunted, dilated, deformed calyces (calyceal clubbing).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1319
text: A child suffering from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis may die  due to:
explanation: The most common and immediate cause of death in children with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is acute heart failure and pulmonary edema secondary to severe hypervolemic fluid overload, or hypertensive encephalopathy.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1288
text: Gross features of renal cell carcinoma include all EXCEPT:
options: It 1s commonly centred in the cortex
It 1s surrounded by a true capsule
explanation: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) typically originates in the renal cortex as a golden-yellow, circumscribed mass with prominent areas of hemorrhage, necrosis, and cystic degeneration, characteristically invading the renal vein.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1294
text: VHL gene mutation may occur in:
explanation: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (the commonest RCC subtype, 70-80%) is strongly associated with loss or inactivation of the VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p, leading to constitutive HIF-1alpha activation and VEGF overexpression.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1295
text: MET proto-oncogene is mutated in:
explanation: Papillary renal cell carcinoma (10-15% of RCCs) is characterized by trisomy 7 and 17 and activating mutations or duplications of the MET proto-oncogene encoding the hepatocyte growth factor receptor.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1287
text: The following tumor is Common in children:
explanation: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common primary malignant renal tumor of childhood (peak age 2-5 years), arising from primitive metanephric blastema and associated with WT1 gene mutations on chromosome 11p13.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1293
text: The blastomatous tissue consists of:
explanation: Classic Wilms tumor exhibits a characteristic triphasic histology consisting of: primitive blastematous sheets of small round blue cells, epithelial tubular/glomeruloid structures, and mesenchymal stroma (spindle cells, skeletal muscle, cartilage).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1321
text: An adult female patient presented with generalized edema. Labarotory  investigations revealed hypoalbuminemia and proteinuria. Renal  biopsy showed diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement  membrane with granular deposits of IgG by immunofluorescence. The  most possible diagnosis is:
explanation: Adult renal oncocytoma is a benign epithelial neoplasm derived from intercalated cells of collecting ducts, characterized grossly by a mahogany-brown color with a prominent central stellate scar, and histologically by sheets of uniform eosinophilic cells packed with mitochondria.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1322
text: A female patient S0 year old presented with oligunia and hematuria.  Kidney function tests revaled increased blood urea. Renal biopsy  showed large subcapsular epithelial crescents in some glomemli. The  renal tubules contained red cell casts. The most possible diagnosis is:
explanation: Renal angiomyolipoma is a benign mesenchymal hamartoma composed of mature adipose tissue, smooth muscle, and thick-walled dysplastic blood vessels, frequently associated with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1281
text: The following type of renal stones usually has a stag horn appearance:
explanation: Staghorn calculi are large branched stones that fill the renal pelvis and calyces, composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite/triple phosphate) caused by urease-producing bacterial infections (Proteus mirabilis).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1282
text: The following type of renal stones is radio-translucent:
explanation: Uric acid calculi develop in acidic urine (pH < 5.5) and are uniquely radiolucent on conventional plain abdominal radiographs (KUB), requiring non-contrast CT for radiographic visualization.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1283
text: The following type of renal stones is multiple and spiky:
explanation: Calcium oxalate calculi are the most common type of urinary stones (70-80%); they are hard, radio-opaque, and frequently have a dark brown, spiky, mulberriform or jackstone appearance that scratches the urothelium causing hematuria.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1297
text: Schistosomiasis of the bladder predisposes to:
explanation: Urinary schistosomiasis (Schistosoma haematobium) causes chronic urothelial ulceration, inflammation, and squamous metaplasia, predisposing heavily to invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) of the urinary bladder.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1299
text: The gross feature of malakoplakia of the bladder mucosa is:
explanation: Malakoplakia of the urinary bladder is an inflammatory pseudotumor associated with chronic E. coli cystitis, characterized histologically by sheets of foamy histiocytes (von Hansemann cells) containing laminated, basophilic, calcified concentric inclusions called Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1303
text: Dye workers are at risk of developing:
explanation: Occupational exposure to aromatic amines (aniline dyes, 2-naphthylamine, benzidine) in textile, chemical, and rubber industries is a major established risk factor for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the urinary bladder.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1307
text: The most improtant prognostic factor in bladder carcinoma is:
explanation: In staging bladder urothelial carcinoma, the single most critical prognostic factor determining survival and management (transurethral resection vs. radical cystectomy) is the depth of tumor invasion into the muscularis propria (detrusor muscle, stage T2).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1354
text: Cryptorchidism means:
explanation: Cryptorchidism refers to the failure of one or both testes to descend completely into the scrotum, arresting in the inguinal canal or abdomen; it causes tubular atrophy, hyalinization, azoospermia, and carries a 3- to 5-fold increased risk of testicular germ cell cancer.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1363
text: Seminoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: It may be of the anaplastic or spermatocytic type
The stroma often shows epithelioid granulomas
explanation: Testicular seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor (peak age 30-40), characterized by sheets of uniform polyhedral cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, prominent nucleoli, and delicate fibrovascular septa infiltrated by T-lymphocytes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1365
text: The following tumor secretes alpha fetoprotein:
explanation: Testicular yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor) is the most common testicular neoplasm in infants and boys under 3 years of age, characterized by elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and pathognomonic Schiller-Duval bodies mimicking primitive glomeruli.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1367
text: The following tumor secretes placental alkaline phosphatase:
explanation: Testicular choriocarcinoma is a highly aggressive malignant germ cell tumor composed of syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts, characteristically producing massive elevations in serum beta-hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) and early hematogenous metastases.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1374
text: The commonest type of malignancy in malignant teratoma is:
explanation: Post-pubertal testicular teratoma is considered malignant regardless of its histological maturity (mature vs. immature components), capable of late aggressive metastasis, unlike benign childhood teratomas.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1356
text: Syphilitic orchitis occurs in:
explanation: Syphilitic orchitis classically presents in tertiary syphilis as a painless gumma or chronic interstitial fibrosis with obliterative endarteritis, characteristically sparing the epididymis (unlike tuberculosis which primarily affects the epididymis).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1357
text: Tuberculous epididymitis results from:
explanation: Tuberculous epididymitis is almost always secondary to retrograde canalicular or hematogenous spread from the urinary tract (kidney/prostate), causing caseating granulomas that begin in the globus minor of the epididymis before invading the testis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1380
text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is explained by the increase in the  following
explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises exclusively in the periurethral and transition zones of the prostate under the trophic hormonal influence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) synthesized by stromal 5alpha-reductase.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1382
text: Perineural invasion is most commonly seen in:
explanation: Perineural space invasion is a characteristic histological hallmark of prostatic adenocarcinoma, where malignant glands wrap around or infiltrate intramural autonomic nerve twigs within the prostatic capsule and periprostatic fat.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1384
text: The following marker is used for diagnosis of prostatic carcinoma:
explanation: Serum Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is an organ-specific (not cancer-specific) serine protease secreted by prostatic epithelial cells; serum levels >4 ng/mL warrant further evaluation, while PSA velocity and free-to-total PSA ratio assist in differentiating BPH from carcinoma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1389
text: Bone metastases from prostatic carcinoma are osteoblastic because the  tumor secretes:
explanation: Skeletal metastases from prostatic adenocarcinoma characteristically stimulate osteoblast proliferation and new woven bone deposition, producing dense, radio-opaque osteoblastic (osteosclerotic) bone lesions on plain radiographs and bone scans.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1397
text: Gleason's grading system for prostatic carcinoma is important for:
explanation: The Gleason grading system for prostatic adenocarcinoma is based entirely on histological architectural growth patterns (patterns 1 through 5) rather than cytological atypia, combining the primary and secondary patterns to yield a prognostic Gleason score.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1399
text: Complications of prostatic hyperplasia include all EXCEPT:
explanation: Major clinical complications of benign prostatic hyperplasia include bladder outlet obstruction, detrusor hypertrophy and trabeculation, bladder diverticula, urinary stasis with recurrent UTIs, bilateral hydronephrosis, and postrenal azotemia.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1404
text: Amale patient 60 year old complained of dysuria and hematuria.  Rectal examination showed enlargement of the prostate. Serum  prostatic specific antigen was normal. The most possible diagnosis is:
explanation: Prostatic adenocarcinoma arises in >70% of cases in the peripheral (posterior) zone of the prostate, which explains why it is palpable on digital rectal examination (DRE) as a hard, irregular nodule before producing early obstructive symptoms.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1426
text: Condyloma accuminatum is not characterised by:
options: It is induced by Epstein Barr virus
It consists of proliferating squamous epithelium
explanation: Condyloma acuminatum of the external genitalia is a benign verrucous squamous papilloma caused by low-risk Human Papillomavirus types 6 and 11, histologically characterized by branching acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and superficial koilocytosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1427
text: Condyloma lata are caused by:
explanation: Condyloma lata are moist, flat, broad, highly infectious mucosal plaques of the vulva, perineum, or scrotum, representing a classical mucocutaneous manifestation of secondary syphilis teeming with Treponema pallidum spirochetes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1429
text: Paget’s disease is a:
explanation: Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva or scrotum manifests as an erythematous, crusted, pruritic plaque, histologically characterized by intraepithelial infiltration of large malignant glandular cells with pale mucinous cytoplasm (mucin-positive, PAS-positive).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1433
text: The following lesion appears as whitish plaques of the vulva:
explanation: Lichen sclerosus of the vulva (kraurosis vulvae) manifests clinically as smooth white porcelain-like atrophic plaques ('leukoplakia'), histologically showing epidermal thinning, hydropic basal degeneration, and a broad band of dense dermal collagen homogenization/hyalinization.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1434
text: The following lesion does NOT predispose to invasive carcinoma:
explanation: Lichen simplex chronicus of the vulva results from chronic scratching or rubbing; it is characterized histologically by marked epidermal hyperkeratosis and acanthosis with regular rete ridge elongation, carrying no intrinsic premalignant potential.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1435
text: Sarcoma botryoides is a type of:
explanation: Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) is the most common malignant vaginal/urinary tract sarcoma in infants and young girls under 5 years, presenting grossly as soft, gelatinous polypoid masses resembling a 'bunch of grapes' protruding from the introitus.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1436
text: The commonest malignant vaginal tumor in childhood is:
explanation: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the penis is strongly associated with lack of neonatal circumcision (poor hygiene/smegma accumulation) and high-risk HPV types 16 and 18, commonly arising on the glans penis or inner surface of the prepuce.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1437
text: The following is NOT a feature of the endocervical polyp:
explanation: Endocervical polyps are benign inflammatory inflammatory outgrowths of endocervical mucosa, composed of loose fibromyxomatous vascular stroma lined by mucus-secreting columnar epithelium, frequently presenting with postcoital spotting.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1439
text: The nuclear features of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia include all  EXCEDPT :
options: Decreased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio   E. Increased mitotic activity
explanation: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is characterized cytologically by nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, coarse chromatin clumping, irregular nuclear contours, pleomorphism, and abnormal mitotic figures starting in the basal layers.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1440
text: Grading of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) depends on:  A Thickness of the epithelium showing loss of maturation
explanation: Histological grading of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia depends on the vertical extent of squamous epithelial dysplasia: CIN 1 involves the lower 1/3; CIN 2 involves the lower 2/3; and CIN 3 involves more than 2/3 to full-thickness dysplasia (carcinoma in situ).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1443
text: The best method used as a screening test for cervical cancer is:
explanation: The Papanicolaou (Pap) cervical cytology smear combined with high-risk HPV DNA co-testing is the worldwide standard screening method, sampling cells from the cervical transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction) to detect pre-invasive dysplastic lesions.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1444
text: Carcinoma in situ means:  A Dysplastic changes involving lower 1/3 of epithelium
options: Dysplastic changes involving lower 2/3 of epithelium
Dysplastic changes involving more than 2/3 of epithelium
Dysplastic changes involving whole thickness of epithelium
Dysplastic changes involving whole thickness of epithelium with  koilocytic changes
explanation: Carcinoma in situ (CIN 3) of the uterine cervix is defined histologically as full-thickness squamous atypia and loss of maturation spanning the entire epithelial height, but strictly contained above an intact basement membrane without stromal microinvasion.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1445
text: HPV induces cervical carcinoma through:  A Induction of koilocytosis
options: Expression of E6 and E7 proteins
explanation: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 induce cervical oncogenesis primarily through integration of viral DNA into host genome, leading to overexpression of oncoproteins E6 (which promotes ubiquitin-dependent degradation of p53) and E7 (which binds and inactivates retinoblastoma pRb).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1511
text: The most important risk factor for cervical cancer is:
explanation: Persistent high-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection (especially genotypes 16, 18, 31, 33, 45) is the single most critical and mandatory epidemiological risk factor for the development of invasive cervical carcinoma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1450
text: The following endometrial changes indicate ovulation:
explanation: Under light microscopy, the histological hallmark confirming normal ovulation and the onset of the endometrial secretory phase is the appearance of uniform subnuclear glycogen vacuoles within columnar glandular epithelial cells on day 16-17.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1456
text: The most important complication of endometrial hyperplasia is:
explanation: Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia carries a <1-3% risk of progression to adenocarcinoma, whereas atypical endometrial hyperplasia (endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia, EIN) carries an alarming 20-30% risk of concurrent or future invasive carcinoma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1457
text: The most common tumor in females is:
explanation: Uterine leiomyoma (fibroid) is the most common benign mesenchymal tumor in women of reproductive age, arising from myometrial smooth muscle cells and characterized by whorled bundles of uniform spindle cells surrounded by a distinct pseudocapsule.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1461
text: Swiss cheese appearance is a feature of:
explanation: Simple non-atypical endometrial hyperplasia characteristically exhibits dilated, cystic, irregular glands lined by non-stratified columnar cells with no cellular atypia, producing a classic 'Swiss-cheese' architectural appearance.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1463
text: Endometriosis is defined as:
options: Presence of endometrial glands in abnormal sites
Presence of endometrial stroma in abnormal sites
Presence of endometrial glands and stroma in abnormal sites
Presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine wall
explanation: Endometriosis is defined pathologically as the presence of functional endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterine cavity, most frequently affecting the ovaries (forming 'chocolate cysts' / endometriomas), pelvic peritoneum, and pouch of Douglas.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1467
text: The most important risk factor for endometrial carcinoma is:
explanation: Type I endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium (accounting for 80% of cases) is strongly driven by prolonged, unopposed hyperestrogenism (obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, estrogen replacement therapy, PCOS) and PTEN mutations.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1469
text: The most aggressive type of endometrial carcinoma is:
explanation: Type II serous carcinoma of the endometrium is an aggressive, estrogen-independent tumor occurring in elderly women with atrophic endometria, strongly associated with TP53 mutations, extensive pelvic dissemination, and poor clinical prognosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1472
text: Hydatidiform mole occurs in:
explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole results from androgenesis: fertilization of an enucleate (empty) ovum by a single sperm that duplicates (46,XX, 90%) or by two sperm (46,XY), producing purely paternal genetic material with no maternal chromosomes.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1473
text: Complete vesicular mole is NOT characterised by:
options: High levels of serum chorionic gonadotropin
Small vesicles in the evacuated mole
explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole is characterized by diffuse, circumferential trophoblastic hyperplasia, generalized hydropic swelling of all chorionic villi with central cistern formation, markly elevated serum beta-hCG (>100,000 mIU/mL), and COMPLETE ABSENCE of fetal or embryonic tissues.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1474
text: Partial vesicular mole is NOT characterised by:
options: Low levels of serum chorionic gonadotropin
Small vesicles in the evacuated mole
explanation: Partial hydatidiform mole results from diandric triploidy: fertilization of a normal haploid ovum (23,X) by two sperm (or a diploid sperm), resulting in a 69,XXX, 69,XXY, or 69,XYY karyotype, and characteristically DOES contain fetal or embryonic parts.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1478
text: Fertilization of normal egg by two spermatozoa results in:
explanation: Fertilization of a normal haploid ovum by two normal spermatozoa produces a triploid (69 chromosomes) conceptus, which pathologically manifests as a partial vesicular mole with scalloped, focal villous edema and identifiable fetal RBCs.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1479
text: The following does NOT show fetal parts:
explanation: In contrast to partial hydatidiform mole or blighted ovum, a complete hydatidiform mole contains NO fetal parts, no umbilical cord, no amniotic membrane, and no nucleated fetal red blood cells within villous capillaries.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1481
text: The following carcinoma is curable:
explanation: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant, invasive epithelial neoplasm composed of anaplastic syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts with extensive hemorrhage and necrosis and NO chorionic villi; it responds spectacularly to chemotherapy (Methotrexate) with >90% cure rates.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1507
text: A 35 year pregnant female suffered from vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound  showed no features. Microscopic exmination of the tissue obtained by  endometrial currettage showed malignant -cytotrophoblast and  syncytiotrophoblast. The most possible diagnosis is:
explanation: Pelvic ultrasonography of a complete hydatidiform mole characteristically displays an enlarged uterine cavity filled with a diffuse, heterogeneous, echogenic mass containing innumerable tiny cystic spaces, termed the 'snowstorm' or 'bunch of grapes' appearance.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1484
text: The commonest site of ectopic pregnancy is:
explanation: Ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized blastocyst implants outside the endometrial cavity, with >95% of cases implanting in the fallopian tube (most commonly in the ampulla), predisposed by chronic salpingitis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1486
text: Stein-Leventhal syndrome consists of all EXCEPT:
explanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS / Stein-Leventhal syndrome) is clinically characterized by hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), chronic anovulation (oligomenorrhea), and bilaterally enlarged ovaries with multiple subcapsular follicular cysts and cortical stromal fibrosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1490
text: Ovarian serous cystadenoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Epithelial lining resembles that of the endometrium
explanation: Serous cystadenoma of the ovary is the most common benign ovarian epithelial neoplasm, typically unilocular, containing clear watery straw-colored serous fluid and lined by a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelial cells resembling tubal mucosa.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1491
text: Ovarian mucinous cystadenoma is characterised by all EXCEPT:
options: Epithelial lining resembles that of the fallopian tube
explanation: Mucinous cystadenoma of the ovary is a multilocular, bulky tumor filled with thick, gelatinous, glycoprotein-rich mucin, lined by non-ciliated columnar epithelial cells with apical mucin vacuoles resembling endocervical or intestinal epithelium.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1493
text: Psammoma bodies may occur in the following ovarian tumor:
explanation: Psammoma bodies are concentric, laminated, basophilic calcospherites that are characteristically found in ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma (as well as papillary thyroid carcinoma and meningioma).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1496
text: The following ovarian tumor secretes oestrogen:
explanation: Granulosa cell tumors of the ovary are sex cord-stromal neoplasms that characteristically secrete estrogens, causing endometrial hyperplasia, irregular uterine bleeding, or precocious puberty; histologically they feature Call-Exner bodies (microfollicles containing eosinophilic fluid).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1500
text: Dermoid cyst of the ovary is a:
explanation: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid cyst) is a benign germ cell tumor composed of well-differentiated tissues derived from all three germ cell layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), characteristically containing hair, sebaceous material, teeth, and keratinaceous debris.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1503
text: Regarding Krukenberg tumors, the following is NOT true:
options: The primary site 1s the gastrointestinal tract
Primary tumor spreads to the ovary by blood
explanation: Krukenberg tumor is a metastatic adenocarcinoma to the ovaries, characteristically bilateral, originating predominantly from gastric signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma (or colon/breast) and histologically displaying mucin-filled signet-ring cells infiltrating ovarian stroma.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1559
text: The ductal-lobular system of the breast is normally lined by:
options: Inner epithelial and outer myoepithelial cells
Outer epithelial and inner myoepithelial cells
explanation: The normal terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) of the human breast is composed of a two-cell epithelial bilayer consisting of: an inner secretory luminal epithelial cell layer and an outer contractile myoepithelial cell layer.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1560
text: The histologic feature of duct-ectasia is:
options: Infiltration of the stroma by polymorphs
explanation: Mammary duct ectasia is an inflammatory condition characterized by dilation of subareolar collecting ducts filled with thick lipid-rich secretions, associated with periductal chronic inflammation rich in plasma cells ('plasma cell mastitis') and periductal fibrosis.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1562
text: Fat necrosis is usually due to:
explanation: Traumatic fat necrosis of the breast typically follows physical trauma or surgery, histologically demonstrating lipid-laden foamy macrophages, foreign body multinucleated giant cells, and central necrotic adipocytes; it can mimic breast carcinoma on palpation and mammography.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1565
text: The histologic features of fibrocystic disease include all EXCEPT:
explanation: Fibrocystic change of the breast comprises a triad of benign non-proliferative alterations: cyst formation (apocrine metaplasia), stromal fibrosis, and adenosis (increased number of acini per lobule).

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1567
text: The following lesion is related to carcinoma:
explanation: Among benign proliferative breast conditions, atypical hyperplasia (atypical ductal hyperplasia, ADH, and atypical lobular hyperplasia, ALH) confers a 4- to 5-fold increased relative risk of subsequent invasive breast cancer.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1568
text: Fibroadenoma is characterised by:
options: Proliferation of the fibrous tissue stroma
Proliferation of both glands and stroma
explanation: Breast fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast neoplasm in young females (age 20-35), presenting as a painless, rubbery, sharply circumscribed, freely movable nodule ('breast mouse') composed of proliferating stromal fibrous tissue compressing glandular ducts.

sources: Pathology/Urogenital Module - MCQ and CASES in Pathology - Dr. Thanaa Helal.pdf-pX-Q1598
text: Phylloides tumor is a:
explanation: Phyllodes tumor (cystosarcoma phyllodes) is a fibroepithelial breast neoplasm characterized by exaggerated leaf-like stromal projections lined by epithelium; it differs from fibroadenoma by possessing hypercellular stroma, and can be benign, borderline, or overtly malignant.
